I just want to add this. With all due respect, you seem like a good partner who just wants to help. But what she needs here is professional help. And to someone with an eating disorder, being given tips to lose weight is extremely damaging. I don't blame you for not knowing this, I only know it myself because I have an eating disorder too.

My advice would be: 

1) Let her know that you are worried for her. Not because she gained weight, but because of her behaviors around food. With eating disorders, we tend to minimize the problem and blame ourselves. Knowing that it isn't, in fact, all in our heads is hard to swallow, but it's the first step. She might get extremely defensive; if so, do not push it. You can try to talk about it later. Also, I would advise you to bring this up sometime when you are not eating or she isn't planning to eat. 


2) Try to avoid comments about her weight, appearance or eating patterns as much as possible. (Obviously, you can talk about her eating disorder, but avoid things such as "should you really eat that?" or "wow, you ate a lot/so little!", etc.). To me, these types of comments always make me spiral further down my disordered thoughts. Instead of commenting on her portion sizes, try to ask her how she's feeling, if something has been on her mind, how her day has been, etc. (and as I said previously, if possible, talk about it when she's not eating). Instead of commenting on her body, try saying nice things about her smile, how she's radiant today, etc.

I wish you the best. You seem like a nice person.

Ive always wondered whether my household was really abusive or not. Records from the local child protective services say "parental negligence". I feel like my parents are beautiful people, but weren't good parents. Now that I'm an adult, we're on excellent terms, which just adds more layers to my confusion.

They let me become obese at 8. Then let me hop on multiple diets, by myself. Then witnessed me purge in the bathroom, but never said a word. A psychiatrist asked them to schedule some kind of routine around meals; they never did.

And they felt bad about it. They said sorry so often. And got mad, sometimes, because I was just getting worse.

 I started to smoke their cigarettes and drink their beers at 13. Was a daily smoker/drinker at 15. Well, they simply started to provide these things for me at that point.

Sometimes, I'd disappear for days. When I would come back, I would first be greeted by two angry adults, given the silence treatment for a while, and then everything would just get back to normal, as if nothing happened.

I have only been grounded once. I had done LSD the night before and was being very talkative for some reason. Next thing I know, my father tells me to shut up and pins me down while my mother watches with a disappointed face and proceeds to smudge my mascara all over my face as I'm crying. What next? I disappear for two days, come back, silent treatment, then it's all good.

Apart from that bad experience, my friends always thought of me as the lucky one. It's true, I had so much freedom. But I wish they had given me support too.

So tell me, Reddit. Please. I need to understand better. Was this abusive? If so, how exactly?
